addedResources.name: Python sys: recursion limit
addedResources.use: Read sys.getrecursionlimit and sys.setrecursionlimit: the limit guards the C stack and its safe maximum is platform-dependent. Check the default with getrecursionlimit (1000 on CPython 3.13), raise it once for memoized DP, or switch to tabulation for deep inputs.

addedResources.name: Erickson lecture note D - Advanced Dynamic Programming
addedResources.use: Read Section D.1 (Saving Space: Divide and Conquer) for the Hirschberg Half-table split that recovers an optimal edit sequence in \(O(m + n)\) space.

addedResources.name: Erickson lecture note J - Approximation Algorithms
addedResources.use: Read Section J.1 (Load Balancing) for the Partition reduction that makes exact scheduling NP-hard, the GreedyLoadBalance heuristic, and Theorem J.1 with its factor-2 proof.

units.title: Dynamic programming states, transitions and base cases
outcomes: Write the state, recurrence, base cases and evaluation order for an unseen optimization problem before coding.
Explain why optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems are both needed, using a negative example.
Prove a recurrence considers every feasible optimum and never admits an invalid solution.
units.why: Every later card asks for the state first. If the state misses information the future needs, no memo or loop order can fix it.

next.note: Fill the recurrence by memo or by table once the state is fixed.
Separate DP recurrences from greedy-choice arguments with proofs or counterexamples.

study.title: Smart recursion first, tables second
study.locator: Section 3.4, The Pattern: Smart Recursion (pp. 105-107): specification plus solution, then subproblems, dependencies and evaluation order

study.title: Text segmentation recurrence
study.locator: Section 3.3 (p. 105): \(\operatorname{Splittable}(i)\) recurrence with base \(\operatorname{Splittable}(n+1) = \text{True}\) and \(O(n^2)\) IsWord calls

study.title: Optimal substructure by contradiction
study.locator: Section 3.7 Edit Distance, Recursive Structure (pp. 111-112): remove the last column of an optimal alignment, and the rest is optimal for the prefixes, proved by contradiction

study.title: The two conditions with a negative example
study.locator: What dynamic programming actually is: optimal substructure plus overlapping subproblems, with merge sort as the negative example
study.depth: The opening says naive fib(43) makes about 433 million calls; that is \(F(43)\), the return value. Erickson Section 3.1 gives the call count \(2F(n+1) - 1\), about 1.4 billion for \(n = 43\).

focus: A state is sufficient when the future depends only on the state, never on how it was reached. \(\operatorname{Splittable}(i)\) needs only the suffix start \(i\).
Optimal substructure is a claim about subproblems: removing the last column of an optimal alignment leaves an optimal alignment of the shorter prefixes.
Base cases define the empty input. \(\operatorname{Splittable}(n+1) = \text{True}\) and \(\operatorname{Edit}(0, j) = j\) are load-bearing, not boilerplate.
Merge sort has optimal substructure without overlapping subproblems, so a memo never hits. Both conditions must hold.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the \(\operatorname{Splittable}\) recurrence with its base case, then run it in Python 3.13 on \(A = \text{ARTISTOIL}\) (\(n = 9\)) with the word set ARTIST, OIL, ART, IS, TOIL: it returns True. Change OR to a sum to count segmentations: 2 (ARTIST.OIL and ART.IS.TOIL).
traps: Adding a state dimension for safety. Extra dimensions multiply the table for no gain; keep the smallest sufficient state.

A state that forgets a constraint the future needs. On a circle of houses (LC 213), \(dp\) over the index alone can rob both the first and the last house; run the line twice, without the first house and without the last, or add "first house robbed" to the state.
Writing the table before the recurrence. Without a one-sentence English specification of the subproblem you cannot tell a wrong recurrence from a wrong loop order.

selfTest.q: Why is \(\operatorname{Splittable}(n+1) = \text{True}\) the correct base case?
selfTest.a: An empty suffix needs no words, so it segments trivially. The recurrence checks \(\operatorname{SplitTable}[j+1]\) for \(j = n\), which reads exactly this cell.

selfTest.q: Merge sort splits, recurses and combines. Why is it not dynamic programming?
selfTest.a: Its halves share no subproblems, so a memo never hits. Optimal substructure alone does not make DP; overlapping subproblems must also hold.

selfTest.q: How does the edit-distance proof show three predecessors are enough?
selfTest.a: By contradiction on the last alignment column: it must be an insertion, a deletion or a substitution. If the remaining prefixes had a shorter edit sequence, gluing the last column back would shorten the whole, contradicting optimality.

selfTest.q: Your recurrence passes the samples but you cannot state its subproblem in one English sentence. What do you do?
selfTest.a: Stop and write the specification first. Without it a wrong recurrence and a wrong loop order look identical in the test output.

units.title: Memoization, tabulation and dependency order
outcomes: Implement memoized and tabulated forms of one recurrence and show they compute the same values.
Read dependencies off a recurrence and state the evaluation order before writing the loop.
Predict when memoized recursion hits the Python recursion limit and switch to tabulation.
units.why: Memoized recursion dies near depth 1000 in CPython. Tabulation with an explicit order is the form that survives production-sized inputs.

next.note: Keep the table when you must reconstruct; compress only the value.
Apply both evaluation forms to two-index recurrences.

study.title: Fibonacci from naive recursion to iteration
study.locator: Section 3.1 (pp. 97-102): RecFibo, the \(T(n) = 2F(n+1) - 1\) call-count argument, MemFibo, IterFibo and IterFibo2
study.depth: Skip Section 3.2, the matrix-squaring speedup (p. 103), until the limits unit.

study.title: The four-step conversion to a table
study.locator: The four-step conversion: dependency DAG, topological order, loop, array; Tracing the table fill on \(n = 8\)

study.title: The default 1000-frame limit
study.locator: sys.getrecursionlimit and sys.setrecursionlimit: the limit guards the C stack, and the highest safe value is platform-dependent. Check the current value with sys.getrecursionlimit() (1000 on CPython 3.13).

focus: Memoization visits states lazily in recursion order; tabulation visits them eagerly in an order you choose. Both compute the same values.
The dependency DAG must be acyclic. For \(\operatorname{fib}(i)\) the edges run to smaller indices, so increasing \(i\) is a valid topological order.
A Python frame per index means depth-\(n\) recursion needs a limit above \(n\). Set it once at module top level, never per function.
State count times per-state work gives total time: \(O(n)\) states at \(O(1)\) each is \(O(n)\) for Fibonacci.
units.reproduce: Closed-book in Python 3.13, write memoized and tabulated fib. Both give \(\operatorname{fib}(25) = 75025\). At the default limit of 1000, \(\operatorname{fib}(2500)\) raises RecursionError; with the limit raised once to 10000 the memoized form returns a 523-digit integer, and the tabulated form returns the same digits. Assert the two results are equal.
traps: Reusing one global memo across calls for state that is not absolute. Stale entries from the previous call return wrong answers; build a fresh memo per call.
Returning a mutable object from a memoized function and letting the caller mutate it. Later cache hits return the mutated object.
Copying a top-down recurrence into a bottom-up loop without flipping the direction. A left-to-right loop reading \(dp[i+1]\) reads uninitialized cells.

selfTest.q: \(\operatorname{fib}(2500)\) under the default limit: what happens and why?
selfTest.a: RecursionError. The chain runs 2500 frames deep before the first base case returns, and the default limit is 1000. The cache cannot help because no call has returned yet.

selfTest.q: When is tabulation better than memoization if both are \(O(n)\)?
selfTest.a: When the topological order is obvious and the input is deep or call overhead matters. Tabulation has no recursion stack and pays one index per step instead of one frame per state.

selfTest.q: Your bottom-up loop reads \(dp[i+1]\) left to right and returns garbage. What went wrong?
selfTest.a: The loop order violates the dependency direction. Either iterate right to left or rewrite the recurrence so it reads already-filled cells.

selfTest.q: Why must a memoized function be pure?
selfTest.a: The cache swaps recomputation for lookup. If the result depends on hidden mutable state, the stored value is stale for the next call and the answer changes.

units.title: Solution reconstruction and rolling state
outcomes: Reconstruct an optimal witness by walking parent pointers back from the answer cell.
Decide whether rolling compression preserves dependencies and reconstruction, and state what is lost.
Implement length-only rolling rows and full-table recovery without mixing the two.
units.why: An optimum without a witness cannot be checked. Compression that deletes the decisions trades checkability for memory.

next.note: Recover witnesses on the string table where ties create several valid answers.
Carry the keep-or-compress decision to grid and interval tables.

study.title: Backtracking the LCS table
study.locator: Recovering the actual subsequence: backtrack from \((m, n)\) with one tie-break used in both passes; \(O(\min(m, n))\) space via row reuse

study.title: Rolling compression and its cost
study.locator: Rolling-pair compression: from \(O(n)\) to \(O(1)\) space, including the warning that compression makes traceback impossible

study.title: Linear-space recovery by splitting
study.locator: Section D.1, Saving Space: Divide and Conquer: forward-backward split with the Half table to recover the edit sequence in \(O(m + n)\) space

focus: Fill and backtrack must share one tie-break. Mixed comparators walk a path the fill never scored.
A rolling row keeps only the previous row, so the parent chain is gone. Length-only compression and reconstruction exclude each other without a Hirschberg split.
Backtrack cost is \(O(m + n)\): every step decrements \(i\), \(j\), or both, so no cell is revisited.
units.reproduce: Closed-book in Python 3.13: fill the LCS table for ABCBDAB vs BDCAB (\(7 \times 5\)) and backtrack to length 4: up-on-ties gives BCAB and left-on-ties gives BDAB, both valid. Then run the rolling length-only form on the same pair and confirm 4.
traps: Keeping one row and then trying to backtrack through it. Old rows are gone; recovery needs the full table or a Hirschberg split.
Using strict greater-than in the fill and greater-or-equal in the backtrack. Either comparator is fine alone; mixing them walks an unscored path.
Reading text1[i] instead of text1[i-1] inside a 1-indexed table. The one-character test (a, a) raises IndexError at \(i = 1\) and exposes the shift.

selfTest.q: Why does the rolling LCS return the length but not the string?
selfTest.a: The backtrack walks rows in reverse, and the rolling form discarded every row but the last two. The parent pointers lived in the discarded rows.

selfTest.q: Two valid LCS strings exist for one input. Is that a bug?
selfTest.a: No. Ties in \(\max(\text{up}, \text{left})\) admit several optimal paths. Any one of them is a correct LCS; enumerating all is a different, exponential-output problem.

selfTest.q: What does the Hirschberg split add over rolling rows?
selfTest.a: The witness in linear space. Rolling rows give the length in \(O(\min(m, n))\) space; the midpoint split recurses on both halves to also recover the sequence in \(O(m + n)\) space at a constant time factor.

selfTest.q: House Robber rolling pair: can you still name the robbed houses?
selfTest.a: No. The pair kept values, not decisions. Keep a boolean choice array or the full dp column to reconstruct the set.

units.title: Sequence and string dynamic programming

Implement LCS, edit distance and quadratic LIS from blank files with differential tests.
Tell subsequence, substring and edit variants apart by their mismatch branch.
units.why: One 2D table shape carries LCS, edit distance and their reductions. The mismatch branch decides which problem you solved.

next.note: Move the prefix-pair machinery to grids and intervals.
Prove the string recurrences and validate them against brute force.

study.title: Two LIS recurrences
study.locator: Section 3.6 (pp. 109-110): First Recurrence: Is This Next? (\(\operatorname{LISbigger}\), two indices) and Second Recurrence: What's Next? (\(\operatorname{LISfirst}\), one index, filled in decreasing order)

study.title: Edit distance recurrence and table
study.locator: Section 3.7 (pp. 111-114): \(\operatorname{Edit}(i, j)\) three-way recurrence, row-major order, and the ALGORITHM vs ALTRUISTIC table with distance 6

study.title: Quadratic LIS with recovery
study.locator: The \(O(n^2)\) LIS: per-index \(dp[i]\) as \(\max\) over smaller predecessors, with parent-pointer recovery and the counting variants

study.title: Prefix decisions with validity gates
study.locator: The recurrence, written once: \(dp[i]\) for the prefix s[:i], a count of decodings for LC 91 Decode Ways and an OR over valid splits for LC 139 Word Break; Why \(dp[0] = \text{True}\), in one trace

focus: \(\operatorname{LISfirst}\) runs on one index because starting here needs only later starts; \(\operatorname{LISbigger}\) needs two indices because skipping is relative to a threshold.
Edit distance has three predecessors because the last column has three shapes. LCS mismatch only skips one side, which is an up or left step.
Subsequence inherits \(\max(\text{up}, \text{left})\) on mismatch; substring resets to 0. On ABCBDAB and BDCAB the answers are 4 and 2.
Decode Ways and Word Break share one skeleton: \(dp[i]\) combines the valid splits that end at \(i\), a sum for Decode Ways and an OR for Word Break, each gated by a validity predicate.
units.reproduce: Closed-book in Python 3.13: \(\operatorname{LCS}(\text{abcde}, \text{ace}) = 3\), \(\operatorname{edit}(\text{horse}, \text{ros}) = 3\), \(\operatorname{edit}(\text{ALGORITHM}, \text{ALTRUISTIC}) = 6\) and \(\operatorname{LIS}([10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18]) = 4\). Then differentially test all three against brute force with Hypothesis on strings over \(\{\text{a}, \text{b}, \text{c}\}\) and lists of length at most 8.
traps: Running LCS code on a longest-common-substring ask. Same table shape, different mismatch branch; the corner cell is not the substring answer.
Forgetting \(\text{max-empty} = 0\) in \(\operatorname{LISfirst}\). Then \(\operatorname{LISfirst}(n)\) needs a special base case instead of falling out of the recurrence.
Counting 06 as one decoding in Decode Ways. A leading zero is invalid; gate 0 and out-of-range pairs to zero.

selfTest.q: State the \(\operatorname{LISfirst}\) recurrence and why decreasing order works.
selfTest.a: \(\operatorname{LISfirst}(i) = 1 + \max\) of \(\operatorname{LISfirst}(j)\) over \(j > i\) with \(A[j] > A[i]\), with \(\text{max-empty} = 0\). Entry \(i\) reads only entries \(j > i\), so filling \(i\) from \(n\) down keeps every read on a computed cell.

selfTest.q: Why does edit distance need the diagonal predecessor while LCS mismatch does not?
selfTest.a: Substitution consumes one character from each string in a single column, which is exactly the diagonal step with cost \([A[i] \ne B[j]]\). LCS mismatch only skips a character from one side, which is an up or left step.

selfTest.q: Word Break on catsandog with [cats, dog, sand, and, cat]: what does \(dp\) say and why?
selfTest.a: False. No valid split covers the string: the \(dp[i]\) OR over splits finds no chain of dictionary words reaching position 9.

selfTest.q: When do you prefer the two-index \(\operatorname{LISbigger}\) over \(\operatorname{LISfirst}\)?
selfTest.a: Rarely for code; \(\operatorname{LISfirst}\) is shorter and \(O(n)\) space. \(\operatorname{LISbigger}\) earns its keep only when the threshold value matters per state, and both are \(O(n^2)\) time.

units.title: Grid, path and interval dynamic programming
outcomes: Derive forward fills for counting and min-sum grids and backward fills for survival predicates.
Derive interval recurrences that try the last operation in \([l, r]\) and fill by increasing length.
Implement both families with brute-force differential tests on small grids and intervals.
units.why: Iteration direction follows the dependency direction. Survival predicates read successors, so the loop runs backward.

next.note: Replace the grid order with post-order on trees.
Move from spatial intervals to capacity and subset state.

study.title: Forward fills and the backward twist
study.locator: The pattern on LC 62 (\(3 \times 7\) worked example, answer 28) and The twist on LC 174 (backward recurrence with the \(\max(\ldots, 1)\) clamp and reversed loops)

study.title: Interval DP with the last operation
study.locator: The pattern: \(dp[l][r]\) tries the LAST operation in the range; Worked example: \(nums = [3, 1, 5, 8]\); What CLRS calls matrix-chain multiplication
study.depth: The chapter labels LC 1039 as Matrix Chain Multiplication; on LeetCode it is Minimum Score Triangulation of Polygon, which has the same interval shape.

study.title: Interval order on optimal search trees
study.locator: Section 3.9 (pp. 117-119): \(\operatorname{OptCost}(i, k)\) interval recurrence and its three valid evaluation orders: by diagonal, row by row from the bottom up, and column by column from left to right

focus: Forward DP fails Dungeon Game because HP-needed-at-entry depends on the suffix, not the prefix. Backward state \(dp[i][j]\) is HP needed on entering \((i, j)\).
The \(\max(\ldots, 1)\) clamp is the survival predicate per cell, not a guard. Dropping it admits zero-HP entries the knight cannot use.
Interval cells depend on strictly shorter intervals, so length-ascending fill is the order. Any single direction that respects shorter-first works.
units.reproduce: Closed-book in Python 3.13: unique_paths(3, 7) = 28, min_path_sum([[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]]) = 7, dungeon([[-2,-3,3],[-5,-10,1],[10,30,-5]]) = 7, burst([3,1,5,8]) = 167. State the grid sizes and all four expected outputs.
traps: Copying the LC 64 idea into Dungeon Game: maximize the path sum, then read the HP it needs. On the problem's own example the max-sum path (down, down, right, right; sum 28) needs 8 HP, but right, right, down, down needs 7.
Continuing the LC 63 base row past the first obstacle. Cells past a top-row wall are unreachable; the base loop must break, not continue.
Filling interval tables row-major left to right. Cell \((l, r)\) reads \((l, k)\) and \((k+1, r)\), which a plain row-major pass may not have written; iterate by length.

selfTest.q: Why does Dungeon Game iterate bottom-right to top-left?
selfTest.a: \(dp[i][j]\) reads \(dp[i+1][j]\) and \(dp[i][j+1]\). Reversed row-major order keeps both reads on computed cells; forward order reads sentinels.

selfTest.q: Unique Paths \(3 \times 7\) is 28. Name the closed form and when it breaks.
selfTest.a: \(C(m+n-2, m-1) = C(8, 2) = 28\). It breaks with obstacles, weights or backward predicates; the DP survives all three.

selfTest.q: Why does Burst Balloons try the last burst in \([l, r]\) instead of the first?
selfTest.a: Bursting \(k\) first changes the neighbors of the rest, so subintervals are not independent. Bursting \(k\) last fixes its neighbors to the interval boundaries, which splits \([l, r]\) into independent \([l, k-1]\) and \([k+1, r]\).

selfTest.q: A forward fill keeps, per cell, the smallest starting HP needed so far. Why can it fail?
selfTest.a: A predecessor that needed less HP so far may arrive with less HP left, and one number cannot keep both. On [[-2,-1,-1],[-3,-1,0],[2,0,-3]] the forward fill answers 8 while the backward fill gives 7.

units.title: Tree dynamic programming
outcomes: Derive per-node state that carries every choice the parent must reason about.
Implement post-order helpers that return tuples or split return-vs-global quantities.
Handle skewed trees within the recursion limit or with an explicit stack.
units.why: On trees the dependency graph is the input. One post-order pass gives linear time; the only design work is the per-node state.

next.note: Trade the tree order for capacity and subset orders.
Prove the per-node recurrence and test it against brute force.

study.title: Maximum independent set on trees
study.locator: Section 3.10 (pp. 120-122): \(\operatorname{MIS}(v)\) recurrence over children and grandchildren, memoization into the tree, post-order evaluation, and the \(\operatorname{MISyes}/\operatorname{MISno}\) mutual recurrence

study.title: Tuple state and the return-vs-global split
study.locator: Two-state DP: the \((\text{rob}, \text{skip})\) tuple on LC 337; The dual-quantity split, with negative values in play, on LC 124 with the \(\max(\text{child\_gain}, 0)\) clamp

study.title: The linear precursor
study.locator: House robber (LC 198): the take-or-skip prototype that LC 337 lifts onto trees, with the [2,1,1,2] parity-greedy counterexample

focus: Single-number returns fail House Robber III because the parent needs both worlds. Return \((\text{rob\_this}, \text{skip\_this})\) and let the parent pick per scenario.
LC 124 returns the straight-down chain but compares the bent path globally. Returning the bent path builds two-bend shapes that are not paths.
Each node is visited once with \(O(1)\) local work, so time is \(O(n)\). Space is the recursion stack \(O(h)\), which is \(n\) on skewed input.
units.reproduce: Closed-book in Python 3.13 with the limit raised once at module top level: rob on level-order [3,2,3,null,3,null,1] = 7 and on [3,4,5,1,3,null,1] = 9. State both level-order inputs and both expected outputs.
traps: Keeping the default limit of 1000 for deep trees. LC 337 allows \(10^4\) nodes and LC 124 allows \(3 \times 10^4\), so a skewed tree raises RecursionError; raise the limit once at module top level or use an explicit stack.
Initializing the LC 124 global to 0. All-negative trees then return 0 for an empty path; start at negative infinity so the root comparison fires.
Recomputing grandchildren per node instead of returning both states. The tuple memoizes both worlds in one pass; without it the recursion revisits subtrees.

selfTest.q: Write the House Robber III recurrence.
selfTest.a: \(\text{rob\_this}(v) = \text{val}(v) + \text{skip}(\text{left}) + \text{skip}(\text{right})\); \(\text{skip\_this}(v) = \max(\text{rob}, \text{skip})\) of each child, summed. Answer \(\max(\text{rob}, \text{skip})\) at the root.

selfTest.q: Why is the empty-subtree identity \((0, 0)\)?
selfTest.a: An empty subtree contributes no income and imposes no obligation, so both slots add zero to the parent sums.

selfTest.q: LC 124: which quantity travels up and why?
selfTest.a: The straight-down chain \(\text{val} + \max(\text{left\_gain}, \text{right\_gain})\). The parent can only extend a linear chain; a bent path extended further would bend twice.

selfTest.q: How does \(\operatorname{MISyes}/\operatorname{MISno}\) relate to the \((\text{rob}, \text{skip})\) tuple?
selfTest.a: It is the same pattern: \(\operatorname{MISyes}(v) = 1 + \sum \operatorname{MISno}(\text{children})\) is \(\text{rob\_this}\), and \(\operatorname{MISno}(v) = \sum \max(\text{yes}, \text{no})\) is \(\text{skip\_this}\).

study.title: Subset Sum and the Nadiria change problem
study.locator: Section 3.8 (pp. 116-117): \(\operatorname{SS}(i, t)\) recurrence with the \(O(nT)\) table, and Exercise 1 Nadiria change (p. 123): greedy failure first, then recurrence, then DP

focus: \(0/1\) sweeps capacity right to left so item \(i\) cannot fund itself in the same pass. Unbounded sweeps left to right so \(dp[a-c]\) already includes item \(i\).
Subset Sum \(O(nT)\) is pseudopolynomial: \(T\) is a value, not the input size. Tabulation loses to backtracking when \(T\) dwarfs \(2^n\).
Bitmask state costs \(2^n\) subsets times \(n\) transitions. It fits only small ground sets; that boundary is the content, not a footnote.
units.reproduce: Closed-book in Python 3.13: coin_change([1,2,5], 11) = 3, coin_change_ii(5, [1,2,5]) = 4, can_partition([1,5,11,5]) = True and can_partition([1,2,3,5]) = False. Also show largest-first greedy on ([1,3,4], 6) gives 3 coins versus optimal 2. State the amounts and all five expected outputs.
traps: Sweeping \(0/1\) capacity left to right. Item \(i\) then reuses its own update and the \(0/1\) table silently becomes unbounded.
Reading min-coins -1 as zero ways. Coin Change returns -1 when unreachable; Coin Change II returns 0 ways. Different families, different sentinels.
Applying bitmask DP past \(n = 20\) without counting. \(2^{20}\) rows times \(n\) columns already exceeds ten million cells; state the bound first.

selfTest.q: Why does the \(0/1\) inner loop run right to left?
selfTest.a: Left to right lets \(dp[a]\) read \(dp[a-c]\) written in the same item pass, reusing item \(i\). Right to left keeps every read on the previous item row.

selfTest.q: Coins [1,3,4], amount 6: what does largest-first greedy give and why is it wrong?
selfTest.a: \(4+1+1 = 3\) coins. Optimal is \(3+3 = 2\). Greedy commits to 4 without comparing the two-coin completion; only the recurrence compares all last-coin choices.

selfTest.q: Subset Sum runs \(O(nT)\). Why is that not polynomial?
selfTest.a: \(T\) measures a value in the input, which takes \(\log T\) bits to write. The bound is polynomial in the numeric value but exponential in the input length.

selfTest.q: When is bitmask state the only state that fits?
selfTest.a: When feasibility depends on exactly which items are used, not just how many or how much. Assignment and visit-all paths need the subset identity itself.

outcomes: Prove a recurrence by induction with the invariant, exchange step or cut property stated, not restated.
Build a Hypothesis harness that compares memoized, tabulated and brute-force results on small inputs.

study.title: Replaying shrunken failures
study.locator: The Hypothesis database; Using @example to run a specific input; Prefer @example over the database for correctness

focus: A proof names the invariant and the step: last-column cases for edit distance, shorter-interval reads for OBST, both worlds for tree tuples.
The harness generates small valid inputs, runs three implementations, and keeps the shrunk failure. Brute force is the oracle, not a fourth opinion.
Derandomize the settings for the reproduce run so the example count and seed replay exactly.
units.reproduce: In Python 3.13 with Hypothesis 6.169 and pytest: @given lists of ints 0-9 with length at most 8, max_examples = 200, derandomize = True. Compare memoized, tabulated and brute-force House Robber on every example: all 200 pass. Then plant the alternating-parity variant: Hypothesis shrinks the failure to [1,0,0,1] with parity 1 versus optimal 2.
traps: Testing only on statement samples. The parity variant passes both LC 198 examples ([1,2,3,1] and [2,7,9,3,1]) and fails first on [1,0,0,1]; generate, do not hand-pick.
Comparing two optimized forms with no brute-force oracle. Agreement proves consistency, not correctness; the exhaustive baseline is the check.
Generating invalid instances such as negative coins or empty grids. Constrain generation to valid inputs or failures indict the generator, not the recurrence.

selfTest.q: What does the edit-distance contradiction actually establish?
selfTest.a: That removing the last column of an optimal alignment leaves an optimal alignment of the prefixes. With the three possible last-column shapes, the three-way min considers every optimum, and each option it considers is a valid alignment.

selfTest.q: Why three implementations instead of two?
selfTest.a: Memoized and tabulated share the recurrence, so a wrong recurrence passes their comparison. Brute force derives from the definition, so it disagrees exactly when the recurrence is wrong.

selfTest.q: Hypothesis shrinks a failure to [1,0,0,1]. What do you do?
selfTest.a: Pin it with @example([1, 0, 0, 1]) so it runs on every test run, then map it to the claim: the alternating pick returns 1, while taking both ends and skipping the middle returns 2, which indicts the parity assumption.

selfTest.q: A proof says by optimal substructure, the recurrence holds. What is missing?
selfTest.a: The argument itself: which cases exhaust the optimum, why the tail is optimal for the subproblem, and why no invalid solution is admitted.

study.title: When exact scheduling is infeasible
study.locator: Section J.1, Load Balancing: NP-hardness by reduction from Partition, GreedyLoadBalance, and Theorem J.1 with its factor-2 proof

focus: DP works on the cell graph because monotone moves or a strict predicate make it acyclic. Arbitrary four-directional movement is not DP.
Coin change is allocation: amount is the budget, denominations are unit costs, and the inner-loop direction is the reuse policy.
Partition makes exact load balancing NP-hard, so the greedy 2-approximation with its stated bound is the honest answer at scale.
units.reproduce: In Python 3.13: longest-prefix-greedy Word Break returns False on \(s = \text{abcd}\) with dict [ab, abc, cd] while tabulated DP returns True. GreedyLoadBalance on jobs [5,5,4,4,3,3,3] with \(m = 2\) gives makespan 15 against optimal 14, inside the factor-2 bound. State both inputs and all three expected outputs.
traps: Calling the greedy 2-approximation optimal. The bound is a worst-case factor, not an equality claim; 15 versus 14 on the demo inputs shows the gap.
Modeling allocation without stating the reuse policy. One loop direction means each unit once; the other means unlimited reuse. Name it.

Running memoized DFS on a cyclic move graph. With four-directional moves and no strict predicate, a call can reach a cell still on the stack, and the memo caches a value computed from an unfinished one. Prove the graph acyclic first, or switch to a shortest-path algorithm.

selfTest.q: Word Break abcd with [ab, abc, cd]: why does longest-prefix greedy fail?
selfTest.a: It takes abc first and strands d. The valid split ab + cd needs the shorter first piece; only the OR-over-splits recurrence compares both.

selfTest.q: Why is load balancing NP-hard, in one reduction?
selfTest.a: Partition reduces to two-machine makespan: the jobs split evenly iff some assignment reaches \(\text{total}/2\). Exact optimization at scale is infeasible, which is why the greedy bound matters.

selfTest.q: State the greedy load-balance bound with its two observations.
selfTest.a: Makespan at most twice optimal. \(\operatorname{OPT}\) covers the longest job and the average load; the last job on the bottleneck machine adds at most one \(\operatorname{OPT}\) to a below-\(\operatorname{OPT}\) base.

selfTest.q: A batching problem has \(10^6\) jobs and 64 machines. Exact DP or greedy?
selfTest.a: Greedy with the stated bound, then measure. Load balancing is NP-hard, so exact search over assignments is infeasible at this size; GreedyLoadBalance is within a factor of 2, and sorting the jobs longest-first tightens the bound.
